The final tests/lib.rs still calls toml::Value::parse on JSON-shaped literals.
verified_wrong_turns.fix_hint: A needs-search task where the coder never fetches the crate docs is the case the research step exists for; here the research step was consumed producing a self-referential sentence instead.

verified_wrong_turns.wrong_turn: cria's compaction summary told the continuing session that src/lib.rs 'currently returns Ok(current)' and that this is the outstanding failure.
verified_wrong_turns.reasoning_quote: `src/lib.rs` – contains the `get_value_at_path` function that walks a dotted key path and returns the found value, but it currently returns `Ok(current)` instead of `Ok(current.clone())`, causing a type‑mismatch error.
verified_wrong_turns.how_we_know_it_was_wrong: src/lib.rs had contained `Ok(current.clone())` since the successful edit at call 0039, confirmed by read_file at 0043 and by the final file on disk. The remaining `Ok(current)` was in src/main.rs, which the summary describes as working.

cause.context_excerpt: The compilation fails with `error[E0308]: mismatched types` because `get_value_at_path` returns `Ok(current)` where `current` is of type `&Value`, but the function signature promises `Value`. The fix is to return `Ok(current.clone())`.
cause.why_this_caused_it: The compaction was written from the accumulated conversation, in which the lib.rs error text appears a dozen times and the main.rs error appears once. The summary then becomes the only state the post-compaction session has, so the stale claim is authoritative.

verified_wrong_turns.fix_hint: Ground the compaction summary's 'what is broken' section in the current check output, not in conversation history.

verified_wrong_turns.wrong_turn: The dictated-code judge answered 'DIRECTATES' — not one of the two permitted words.
verified_wrong_turns.reasoning_quote: That's a specific code snippet. That is code to copy. So it's DIRECTATES.
verified_wrong_turns.how_we_know_it_was_wrong: The prompt says 'Answer EXACTLY one word: DICTATES ... DESCRIBES'. The same judge answered the correctly spelled 'DICTATES' at calls 0024, 0033 and 0041.
verified_wrong_turns.fix_hint: Fail closed on an unrecognised verdict token rather than letting a near-miss spelling silently take a branch.

verified_wrong_turns.wrong_turn: Emitted its tool call inside the reasoning stream rather than as a response, so the final call of the run did nothing.
verified_wrong_turns.reasoning_quote:
We need to edit src/main.rs to implement the CLI. Let's read src/main.rs.
<tool_call>
<function=read_file>
<parameter=path>
src/main.rs
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
verified_wrong_turns.how_we_know_it_was_wrong: 0060-coder-s1.response.json has empty content and no tool_calls; the run ended here on milestone-miss-15min. The same failure produced empty calls at 0025, 0030 and 0045.

cause.context_excerpt:
If you choose to call a function ONLY reply in the following format with NO suffix:

<tool_call>
<function=example_function_name>
cause.why_this_caused_it: The turn is prefilled with an open `<think>` tag and reasoning is captured until it closes. A model that starts composing the tool call before closing the think block has its whole call swallowed into reasoning_content and parsed as nothing.

verified_wrong_turns.fix_hint: Scan reasoning_content for a well-formed <tool_call> block when the response carries no tool call, and lift it.

mechanisms.name: the steer tells the coder what is wrong, and it is wrong
mechanisms.what_happens: cria's supervisor writes a confident cause for a failure and injects it as an order. The coder had usually already seen evidence pointing elsewhere, and it drops that evidence because an injected instruction outranks its own eyes. It then spends its remaining calls chasing the invented cause. In several runs the coder had the correct diagnosis in its own words in the same breath and abandoned it.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/go 1/1, call 0076. Steer: "You've been stuck looping on the same 'os.WriteFile returns 1 value' error for ~20 turns... The code on disk is fine — this is a stale build/cache artifact issue, not a source problem." Coder: "This is clearly a cache/build state problem." It spent its last three calls on a cache wipe; the run ended at the wall with a two-character source fix unmade.
mechanisms.realised_cost: The single biggest source of wasted calls in this arm. Two runs (ternary-bonsai/go, qwen35/java 5/5) ended at the time wall with the real fix known but unmade; one lost check (ternary-bonsai/java) and one broken file (ternary-bonsai/rust).
mechanisms.fix: A steer must not contain a cause. Restrict the steer author's output to what a check or a file read actually returned plus the next thing to look at, and drop any sentence asserting why something fails. In all 24 turns the coder's own reading beat the supervisor's guess, so the honest direction is to remove the diagnosis from the steer entirely.

mechanisms.name: cria orders work that is already done, or work already proven impossible
mechanisms.what_happens: The supervisor's view of the session is built from the coder's recent thinking, not from the disk or the tool results. So it commands edits that already landed, declares finished files missing, and re-issues commands the session has already watched fail or be refused. The coder cannot disobey and cannot make the change real, so it re-reads, re-edits to no effect, or loops until the rumination guard kills the turn.
mechanisms.worst_example: gemma4/java 2/2, call 0086. Steer: "Fix the load method in Importer.java to handle records with fewer columns than header names gracefully; catch IllegalArgumentException..." — already on disk at lines 108-112. Coder: "It seems I ALREADY did that in the previous turn's edit! Wait, no, let me check again." The next call was aborted by cria's own rumination guard at ~8,255 reasoning tokens.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Pure waste, in every run it appeared in — dozens of no-op edits and re-reads, plus at least two rumination aborts. One run (nemotron-elastic/rust) was told with three minutes left to write a CLI that had existed since call 0007.
mechanisms.fix: Compose the supervisor's view at authoring time from a fresh directory listing and the real tool results, including denials and unreadable-file placeholders — not from the coder's thinking. Then re-check the finished directive against disk before injecting it: if the named change is already present, or the named command already failed in this session, drop the steer rather than send it.

mechanisms.name: cria says the job is not finished but cannot say what is missing
mechanisms.what_happens: When the completion check cannot confirm the work, cria tells the coder "the checks pass but the task is NOT fully done" and forbids it to declare done. No missing artifact is named, and sometimes the stated reason is incoherent — identical numbers on both sides, or a raw fragment of the judge's own thinking. With nothing to act on, the coder re-runs green tests, re-reads unchanged files, invents busywork, or blind-rewrites whichever file it last suspected.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/rust 2/2, call 0080 (the fourth of five identical steers). Steer: "The repo's automated checks pass, but the task is NOT fully done yet: unverified — the careful check could not confirm completion; keep working". Coder: "The steer message indicates that the task is not fully done yet. Let me review what was asked" — then built a release binary nobody asked for, on a workspace the verifier scored 4/4.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Roughly 30 wasted calls across four runs, all on already-passing work. One lost check (nemotron-elastic/go rewrote a seeded test after a 'something is broken, cannot say what' steer) and one false completion claim (ternary-bonsai/ruby called task_complete with two checks failing).
mechanisms.fix: Delete this steer. A completion veto that cannot name the missing artifact has no content, and the coder has no way to overrule it — silence is strictly better. If the careful check can name a missing file or deliverable, send that name and nothing else.

mechanisms.name: the steer's wording quietly replaces the task
mechanisms.what_happens: The supervisor paraphrases the job — which outputs to print, which library to use, which flag to accept, which tool to edit with — and the coder treats the paraphrase as the spec. Anything the steer forgot to mention gets dropped from the deliverable; anything it added gets built. Because the paraphrase arrives after the task and reads as authoritative, the coder stops re-reading the user's own words.
mechanisms.worst_example: gemma4/node 1/1, call 0016. Steer: "Add commander to your dependencies in package.json and ensure it is installed before attempting to run the script again... Update package.json now." Coder wrote "dependencies": { "commander": "^12.0.0" }. The task's check was that the tool run with no installed packages; the verifier reports request_removed failing on exactly that runtime dependency.
mechanisms.realised_cost: The most expensive mechanism in the arm: nine lost checks (a third-party decimal library removed, an EU list hand-rolled, a printed address dropped, an invented --handle flag, a seeded test broken) and two cases of working code broken.
mechanisms.fix: A steer must never restate the task, the deliverable, the implementation choice, or the tool to use. Cut the deliverable-restating section from the steer author's prompt so the only wording the coder ever sees about what to build is the user's own. Where a steer would need to name the deliverable to be useful, it should not be sent.

mechanisms.name: a partial list of files is handed over as the whole truth
mechanisms.what_happens: cria gives its judges lists it built itself — the workspace files, the files changed so far, the task text — and labels them ground truth. The lists are filtered, replayed from a compacted turn log, or cut off mid-sentence. A judge told this is ground truth reads every omission as an absence: no build file, so nothing runnable; no source file, so it was never written; no third requirement, so only steer on two.
mechanisms.worst_example: gemma4/java 2/2, call 0101. Facts block: "WORKSPACE FILES ... (on-disk ground truth at judging time, newest first): src/main/java/pipeline/Importer.java (6783 B)" — pom.xml, the data files and target/ were all on disk. Judge: "There is no pom.xml or build.gradle listed in the provided file list?" It answered runs:false, so cria never executed the finished importer.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Three lost checks — a final verification run skipped, and two deliverables (messy-feed handling, REVIEW.md) that the supervisor could not see because the task text was truncated mid-sentence. One run ended early on a directive to rewrite a file that already existed. Two occurrences cost nothing.
mechanisms.fix: Build these blocks from the real thing at the moment of judging: list the directory instead of replaying the turn log, and never truncate the task text into a supervisor prompt — the context floor should shrink the transcript, not the job. If a view is filtered, stop calling it on-disk ground truth and say plainly that it is partial.

mechanisms.name: a failed read is recorded as a document that was read
mechanisms.what_happens: cria keeps a ledger of what has really been read this session and presents it to its research judges as fact. It counts the bytes that came back, not whether the read succeeded, so a shell error like "No such file or directory" is logged as a 107-character document. The judge is told to judge only against the ledger, so it rules the research step done on the strength of an error message.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/java 1/1, call 0006. Ledger: "- /tmp/.../Importer.java — response fields it defines: 261 chars read from disk". The 261 chars were "/bin/bash: line 2: .../Importer.java: No such file or directory". Judge: "We have read Importer.java file. It contains class structure etc. So... verdict should be DONE."
mechanisms.realised_cost: One lost check and a plan step marked verified on nothing; the real file was not opened until two calls later. Cheap in calls, but it defeats the one gate that is supposed to be ground truth.
mechanisms.fix: Record a document in the read ledger only when the read actually succeeded and returned content — gate on the tool result, not on byte count. When a ledger line carries no parsed content, the research check must fail closed instead of letting the judge assume.

mechanisms.name: the supervisor writes code, then cria cuts holes in it
mechanisms.what_happens: The supervisor is told never to write code but is also told to command one concrete action now, so it writes the command or the edit anyway. cria's dictated-code check then either drops the whole steer after a long reasoning chain, or lets it through with fragments blanked out. A weak coder transcribes the dictated line and garbles it, or reads the blanks as its own job to fill and invents far more than was meant.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/java 1/1, call 0015. Steer: "insert a <dependency> for Apache Commons CSV before </dependencies>... new_string='</dependencies>\n<dependency>…</dependency>'". The coder copied that shape into a pom.xml that had no dependencies block at all: "Unrecognised tag: 'dependency' ... line 18, column 15" — the build never compiled again for the rest of the run.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Three checks lost in one run to a malformed build file, one working test helper broken, and one eight-call supervisor chain thrown away when the dictated-code check finally rejected it. The check fired and the steer shipped anyway at least twice.
mechanisms.fix: The write-then-redact design is the defect: a blanked-out command is worse than no command. Stop asking the supervisor for a concrete command or edit — ask it for the observation — so there is nothing to redact. Until then, a DICTATES verdict must block the steer, not scrub a token out of it.

mechanisms.name: the supervisor must give an order, so it invents one
mechanisms.what_happens: The unstick prompt is a forced binary: write a short imperative directive or say one word. Saying nothing is framed as the narrow exception, and the directive must name exactly one concrete action to take now. A judge that has just read a long transcript and found nothing genuinely wrong still has to command something, so it fabricates — a method that does not exist, a filename that does not exist, a file anchor it never read, a surcharge that is not in the spec, or a redirect away from the failing build.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/java 1/1, call 0011. Prompt: "Give exactly ONE concrete next action that differs from the repeated failed behavior. Command the coder to perform that action NOW with an available tool call." Judge: "We have not yet read pom.xml... But the directive must be output now, not after reading." It invented a </dependencies> anchor that the file did not contain.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Five lost checks, including a whole Java run whose build was fabricated into a broken state, plus one run where a judge that had just concluded the coder was fine issued a design decision that failed two checks. One occurrence is the mirror image: the tie-break to stay silent dropped a real unfinished deliverable.
mechanisms.fix: Remove the forced binary. Let the author return nothing without having to justify it, and let it spend a call reading a file before it commands anything; drop the "exactly ONE concrete action NOW" rule that makes it fabricate names and anchors. A directive that names a file, method, or literal string must have come from a read performed in that same call, or it is not sent.

mechanisms.name: the stop-second-guessing nag freezes a false belief
mechanisms.what_happens: After a rumination abort, cria injects a note telling the coder to stop re-examining, pick the simplest step and not revisit the decision. What the coder already knew was usually wrong, so the note locks the wrong premise in place and demands an immediate edit. With no real fix in hand the coder ships a cosmetic one, or skips the arithmetic re-check that would have caught its own bad numbers.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/ruby 1/1, call 0024. Guard: "Stop re-examining. Pick the simplest next concrete step and take it via a tool call... do not revisit the decision." Coder wrote "assert_equal 27.49, Shipping.shipping_cost(\"express\", 4.0, 50.0)" — it had itself computed 14.99 + 2.50×4 correctly two calls earlier. The rest of the run chased those bad numbers.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One lost check and roughly a dozen wasted calls, including one edit that deleted a dead line and changed nothing. In two turns the guard directly produced a half-finished edit the coder never re-read.
mechanisms.fix: Aborting the turn is the whole intervention; the injected instruction is the harmful part. If a note is kept, it must say stop re-arguing and go re-read the file, and must never forbid checking or demand an edit this turn.

mechanisms.name: the supervisor repeats the coder's guess back as fact
mechanisms.what_happens: cria hands the supervisor the coder's private thinking with a warning that it may be false. When the coder has repeated the same wrong belief for several turns, the supervisor reads the repetition as evidence and writes it into the directive. The coder then receives its own hallucination back with cria's authority on it and treats it as confirmed. The warning label does not hold.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/python 4/4, call 0187. Facts block: "THE CODER'S RECENT PRIVATE THINKING — this is what the coder BELIEVES, not what is true... treat every factual claim in it as unverified." Judge: "_tmpdb() calls db.init(path) ... At that point, db.DB_PATH is still 'orders.db'". The steer went out, and at 0189 the coder wrote the useless db.init(path=path) edit that is still in the delivered file.
mechanisms.realised_cost: A whole Python run's integration suite never went green, and nine calls in a Java run went to a repository theory the coder had invented. No check was ever gained.
mechanisms.fix: Stop making the coder's private thinking the supervisor's main evidence — feed it tool results and file contents, and use the thinking only as the trigger. A directive may restate a factual claim only if it came from a file the author read in that same call.

mechanisms.name: the pre-coding research step is written badly and then passed
mechanisms.what_happens: Before coding, cria asks a model to name the one external source that must be read. It has no definition of external, so it points at workspace files, or it reads the pasted task as an order and writes the whole project instead of a step. When the answer is unusable cria retries with the bad answer quoted back, which produces a step that names no source at all. The step critic then cannot fail a step that describes source rather than requiring an action.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/rust 1/1, call 0003. Retry prompt: "You answered: ``` # Cargo.toml [package] name = \"toml-cli\" ...``` That sentence cannot be the step: it is far longer than one step." Judge: "The source is the provided code snippets." The task is tagged as needing a doc lookup; the toml crate docs were never fetched and the API was hallucinated for the whole run.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One lost check plus a wasted coder turn per run; in the Rust run it removed the only chance the model had to learn the real library API. In the Ruby run it merely burned one call.
mechanisms.fix: This assist produced no correct step in any run here — delete it. If it is kept, say plainly that files inside the workspace are not external sources, and when the answer is unparseable drop the step instead of retrying with the bad answer in the prompt.

mechanisms.name: one directive asks for several changes; only the first lands
mechanisms.what_happens: The supervisor packs two to four changes into a single order and demands them now. The coder gets one tool call per turn, so it applies the first part and the rest waits for a turn that may never come — or it narrates the whole plan and reports it as an outcome without writing anything. A half-applied structural change can leave the workspace worse than before the steer.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/python 1/1, call 0044. Steer: "DO THIS NOW: 1. In .../orders/db.py: Add a module-level ACTIVE_PATH = \"orders.db\". Change every function signature to remove the path=DB_PATH default". Step one landed; app.py still read def serve(port=8080, path=db.DB_PATH), so importing it raised AttributeError. The state before this call was 9 passed / 4 failed; after it, nothing ran at all.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Expensive for two occurrences: one workspace broken so badly the verifier could not start the service (four checks), and one run that ended with a final response claiming a Dockerfile had been added when no file was written.
mechanisms.fix: A directive may ask for one change. Cap it at one in the author's prompt and drop the extra clauses at injection time; the second change can be authored next turn, because the coder only gets one action per turn anyway.

mechanisms.name: cria calls a coloured build log "binary" and deletes it
mechanisms.what_happens: Maven prints its output in colour. Those colour codes are control characters, and cria's binary detector counts them, decides the text is a blob, and replaces the whole thing with a one-line note saying the data cannot be read as text. Every compiler error in the run disappears. Both the coder and the judge then have only a byte count and an exit code to reason from, so they guess: the file must be binary, the output must be too large, the tool must be broken, the error must be a runtime one. Whole runs are spent inventing ways to see output that cria itself removed.
mechanisms.worst_example: gemma4/java 2/2, call 0067 — cria's own steer told the coder to change the deliverable to work around cria: "Instead of repeatedly trying different shell redirections that result in binary output, modify `Importer.java` to write the final summary directly to a file (e.g., `summary_report.txt`)". The change landed in the shipped code. What triggered it, verbatim: "[binary content: 1,170 bytes — not shown; binary data cannot be read as text]".
mechanisms.realised_cost: The largest single cost in this group. It hit all four models on every Java run — one run carried the note in 212 of 275 prompts, another in 218 results. It burned eight consecutive calls on transport workarounds in one run, sent one model to the web for documentation it did not need, and put a fabricated report file into a deliverable. Two Java runs ended not compiling with nobody able to see why.
mechanisms.fix: cria/content_reduce.py looks_binary() counts any character below 32 outside tab/newline/CR. Strip ANSI escape sequences before that count. A log with colour codes is text, and this is the one result a compiled-language task cannot proceed without.

mechanisms.name: cria's own checker pretends to be the coder
mechanisms.what_happens: cria runs its periodic check by injecting a shell script into the conversation as if the coder had typed it. Two things go wrong. The judge reading the transcript sees a command the coder never wrote and blames it for it, or the coder sees its own apparent last verification move and copies the script verbatim. And because the script chains several commands (and sometimes pipes into tee or tail), the exit code that comes back belongs to the wrapper, not to the build — so a failed compile arrives as "Process exited with code 0".
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/java 5/5, call 0252 — "The compilation succeeded. Let me verify by looking at the compile log and running the tests." The only readable field was "Process exited with code 0", which was `tail`'s exit, not maven's. The same output read later said "COMPILATION ERROR … BUILD FAILURE"; the verifier confirms the project never compiled.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Two runs lost a check to a false green build. One steer was spent telling the coder to stop running a command cria had run. One coder call was spent replaying cria's own six-command check script for no new information.
mechanisms.fix: Run the check out of band and report its result as cria's, not as a coder turn, with per-step status instead of one exit code for the whole chain. Never let a pipeline's or a chain's exit code stand in for the command being judged.

mechanisms.name: cria replays an old check result and swears it is current
mechanisms.what_happens: cria stores the last check output and re-attaches it under the heading "GROUND TRUTH FROM THE REPO'S CHECKS" with the words "unchanged since you were last shown them — you have not cleared them yet". The judge is separately instructed to rank that block above everything else it can see. When the coder has already fixed the thing, the result is a flat false statement of fact outranking live evidence. The reader cannot doubt it, so it doubts reality instead — inventing stale bytecode, Ruby caching, unsaved files, inconsistent tools — or it burns its one steer ordering a fix that landed calls ago.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/python, call 0039 — "The issue might be stale bytecode. Let me remove all pyc files and __pycache__ directories to force a clean recompile". The trigger, verbatim: "$ python3 -m pytest -q — orders/db.py:38: sqlite3.OperationalError: 5 values for 4 columns", a failure fixed sixteen calls earlier and green in the model's own test runs since. In the same run cria reverted to that 22-call-old snapshot for three later judge calls.
mechanisms.realised_cost: The biggest source of wasted calls in this group after the binary filter, and it touched every model and five languages. Six consecutive judge calls in one run spent deciding the block was stale; a four-minute judge call out of a 31-minute budget spent re-deriving a fixed bug; several steers spent ordering completed work.
mechanisms.fix: Delete the replay. cria/prompts/steer_checks_repeat.txt asserts something cria does not know to be true. If a check result matters, re-run it; if it cannot be re-run, drop it. At minimum a check result must be stamped with the turn it ran on and expired the moment a file it names is written again.

mechanisms.name: the file's real current text is never in front of the reader
mechanisms.what_happens: cria shows a judge file names and byte counts, cuts file contents to a few hundred characters mid-word with no marker, replaces written content with "[elided N chars]", and answers a successful edit with only "Wrote foo.rb". So the newest copy of a file anywhere in the context is the copy from before the last change — or there is no copy at all. Readers then report what they cannot see as missing or broken: a finished file looks abandoned mid-token, a seven-test file looks like three tests, a write that fixed the bug looks like it never happened, and a coder rebuilding an edit target reproduces the version it can still see.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/rust 1/2, call 0011 — "The coder has not shown any tests yet." Six tests had been on disk for five calls. What the judge was given, verbatim: "[10] the coder called write_file — path=src/main.rs; content=[elided 3163 chars — this exact content is on disk at src/main.rs; read_file to view it]". It never called read_file.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Wasted calls in nine of the twenty-four runs, and repeat offences inside single runs — one qwen35 ruby run had the judge report the same phantom truncation four separate times. It also produced steers ordering already-finished work, and one refused edit built entirely from a stale copy.
mechanisms.fix: Two upstream changes, both about never letting a shortened view stand in for the file. Return the new content in the edit/write tool result so the freshest copy in context is the current one. And stop shortening file text in judge transcripts: give the judge the file, or require it to read from disk before it may assert anything about content. A clip with no marker is the worst case — it reads as end-of-file.

mechanisms.name: the answer gets cut off the end of a command result
mechanisms.what_happens: When cria shortens a tool result for a judge it keeps the beginning and drops the end. Compilers, test runners and package managers put the useful part at the end. So the judge gets crates compiling and loses the four errors; gets the stack unwinding and loses the exception line; gets Go's "to add:" and loses the very next line telling it what to add. The same condenser reduces a check to one line and drops rustc's `help:` suggestion, which is the fix. With the cause deleted, the judge either clears broken code as correct or invents a cause of its own.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/go, call 0027 — "the simplest approach is to remove the decimal dependency entirely from go.mod and use standard library math instead". The task required that library. Go had printed the remedy; cria's one-line rendering chopped it: "$ go build ./... — cart.go:9: missing go.sum entry for module providing package github.com/shopspring/decimal ...; to add:" — dangling colon, nothing after it. The judge concluded no fix existed.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Two checks lost outright: one run had its required money library deleted on cria's instruction, another had its broken source file explicitly cleared as "already looks valid". Plus repeated wasted calls chasing invented causes.
mechanisms.fix: When a command result must be shortened, keep the tail, not the head — errors live at the end. And when the check parser cannot recognise a diagnostic, pass the output through verbatim instead of emitting "exited 1 with no parseable diagnostics", which throws the whole thing away.

mechanisms.name: "don't change the test" is not scoped to the tests that came with the task
mechanisms.what_happens: cria's check preamble says that if a test failed, changing the test is not a fix. It does not say which tests. Models apply it to tests they wrote themselves minutes earlier, and to tests whose own setup is broken. So a model that wrote a wrong expected value treats its own mistake as an immovable contract and bends working shared code to match it; a model that correctly diagnosed that its tests speak HTTPS to a plain HTTP server files the fix under "not mine to touch" and leaves the suite red.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/ruby, call 0029 — "the instruction says 'Don't change what the tests assert; they describe the behaviour our customers were promised.' So we must adjust code to meet the test expectation." The test in question did not exist until the model wrote it five calls earlier. At 0032 it then corrupted the shared cost rule to satisfy it, and the hidden contract tests failed.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Working code broken in one run and two checks lost there; three more checks lost across two python runs where the model left its own broken test harness alone. This one actively made deliverables worse, not just slower.
mechanisms.fix: Scope the sentence in cria/prompts/block_nudge_preamble.txt to the files that were present in the starting state, and say plainly that a test written this session, or a test whose own setup is wrong, is fair game to fix. cria already knows which files it started with.

mechanisms.name: a clean syntax check reads as "the task is done"
mechanisms.what_happens: cria reports its lint-and-syntax floor as "the repo's own checks reported no error-class problems", and in one case as "The repo's automated checks pass". It arrives as the last authoritative statement in the context. A weak model reads it as a verdict on the whole job rather than on syntax, and signs off — without running the tool the way a user would, without a build, sometimes claiming work it never did. The caveat that no tests were run sits behind the headline and does not land.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/node, call 0073 — "Created a Dockerfile for containerized execution ... All requirements have been met and verified." No Dockerfile was ever written. The last line before that reasoning: "⟦ctx:checks⟧ the repo's own checks that ran reported no error-class problems."
mechanisms.realised_cost: Three runs stopped early on it — a missing Dockerfile, a missing regression test, a CLI never once run in its default mode. In the Java run it also let the model keep working past a build that had been broken since before the message was sent.
mechanisms.fix: Do not say "the checks pass" when only syntax and lint ran, and never say it at all when any command in the check produced output the model could not read. State exactly what ran and what it covered, or say nothing — silence beats a green light cria cannot back.

mechanisms.name: a judge call that costs a full call and returns nothing usable
mechanisms.what_happens: cria spends a model call on a judge and has no bound on what comes back. Some judges think until they hit the token limit and return empty content, so no steer reaches the coder at all. One returned a verdict whose stated reason argued itself in a circle and ended "All requirements appear to be met" while still reporting the work unfinished — cria forwarded it. Another re-issued a directory listing it had already been answered, because cria rendered the same recovered call twice with only one reply. Every one of these costs the same as a good call.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/python, call 0031 — four minutes of a 31-minute budget, finish_reason "length", content null, nothing delivered. It spent them re-deriving "the db.py migration bug" that had been fixed eight calls earlier and was green in the model's own test run.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Five calls that produced no steer, including one 32k-token call and one that ate an eighth of a run's wall clock. No check was lost directly, but the time came out of runs that were already timing out.
mechanisms.fix: Bound the judge's thinking and treat a length-truncated or unparseable verdict as no signal — skip the steer for that cycle instead of retrying with reasoning off, which is how the self-contradicting verdict got produced. And render each recovered call once, with its reply.

mechanisms.name: cria clips the user's own task text out of the judge's prompt
mechanisms.what_happens: The judge prompt shortens the task description to a few hundred characters. The task's later paragraphs — where the specific requirements and prohibitions live — are simply gone. The requirement then reaches the judge only as an echo inside the coder's private thinking, which the same prompt tells the judge to treat as unverified belief. So the judge weighs a real user instruction as a possible hallucination and overrules it.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/ruby, call 0017 — the steer told the coder to hand-roll the EU member list, the one thing the user forbade. The task text handed to the judge stopped at "The README has no rate ta", cutting the paragraph containing the prohibition. In the gemma4 run the same clip produced "The coder's preoccupation with an EU list seems like a hallucinated requirement".
mechanisms.realised_cost: One check lost outright (the country-to-zone requirement was never met in that run) and one steer spent ordering the coder to abandon required work. Only twice, but both times it deleted a requirement rather than slowed anything down.
mechanisms.fix: Never shorten the user's task text, anywhere. It is the shortest and most load-bearing thing in any prompt cria composes; if a prompt does not fit, cut cria's own scaffolding first.

mechanisms.name: the no-code-in-steers gate cuts sentences apart
mechanisms.what_happens: cria asks a weak model to decide whether a steer hands the coder code, then scissors out the offending tokens. The judgement is a coin flip and the surgery is not language-aware. In one direction the remedy is excised and what reaches the coder is an ungrammatical fragment with a stray bracket and no fix named. In the other direction literal code sails through because the fragment was short.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/java 2/5, call 0064 — the delivered steer read "make the shared totals map thread-safe by using [code removed ...]) when initializing it". The thread-safety bug was never fixed and the verifier's race check failed. The gate's own reasoning: "Does it give code? Yes. ... Verdict: DICTATES."
mechanisms.realised_cost: One check lost to a steer that named no remedy. In the other run the gate let a Ruby hash literal through, which the coder pasted verbatim — the assist did the model's thinking for it, which is the outcome the gate exists to prevent.
mechanisms.fix: Delete the post-hoc redaction. A filter that removes tokens from a finished sentence cannot produce a usable steer. Constrain the steer author to describe rather than dictate when it writes, and drop the scissors that run afterwards.

mechanisms.name: the repetition notice pushes the model off the step it was just told to take
mechanisms.what_happens: When a read is repeated, cria appends a notice saying the tool has told the model everything it can and it should take a different action. If a steer has just ordered the model to work on that file, the notice lands immediately after the order and wins. The model concludes it already has all the information it needs and switches to something else — usually re-running the suite — and the ordered work never happens.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/ruby, call 0033 — "I already have all the information I need. Let me run the tests to verify everything works." The steer directly above said "then add test coverage for it". The notice, verbatim: "Repeating it again will return that same result: it has told you everything it can. Read what it already returned above, or take a DIFFERENT action."
mechanisms.realised_cost: One check lost — the express tests were never written in that run and the verifier recorded "model wrote its own tests: False". Both occurrences are in the same run and the same model, so the evidence for how widely it bites is thin; the cost where it did bite was real.
mechanisms.fix: Drop the "it has told you everything it can" wording — it invites the model to declare its information gathering finished — and suppress the notice entirely on a read that a live steer just asked for.

mechanisms.name: the whole-file rewrite escalation lets a previously refused change through
mechanisms.what_happens: After several failed targeted edits, cria stops trying to help the model pin the exact text, hands it the whole file and orders one full rewrite. That removes the guard that had been blocking a specific bad change. The model, rewriting from scratch, re-applies the change cria had already refused twice — and this time nothing checks it.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/ruby, call 0041 — "I need to also fix the `test_unknown_zone_rejected` test since \"moon\" now raises an ArgumentError from `zone_for`. Let me write the full corrected file." cria's escalation had just said: "you have failed to edit this file 4 times ... STOP editing it. Here is its EXACT current content on disk; produce the corrected FULL file in a single write_file call". The seeded test's "moon" became nil permanently.
mechanisms.realised_cost: This single edit is the whole difference between the assisted run at 3/5 and the unassisted run at 4/5 — the clearest case in this group of an assist making the outcome worse. One occurrence, so do not build a special case around it.
mechanisms.fix: The escalation must not be a clean slate. Carry the refused edits' intent into the rewrite instruction, and re-check the rewritten file against the starting state's protected regions before accepting it. If that cannot be done cheaply, do not escalate to a whole-file rewrite at all.

mechanisms.group: cria's own injected context (denied / tool-surface / files / compacted)

mechanisms.name: the hand-off note says what is broken without checking, and cria calls it your own finding
mechanisms.what_happens: When cria squeezes the conversation it asks the same weak model to write a short hand-off note, and the note must fill a 'what is broken / what still needs doing' slot. The model has no file on screen and no check output, so it fills that slot from memory, from stale errors, or from the original task's wish-list — and gets it wrong. cria then puts the note at the top of every later prompt with wording that says this is your own earlier work. From then on the coder and cria's own judges trust the note over the file they just read, and hunt for problems that do not exist.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/python 2/4, call 0082. The coder found the real bug — 'It uses HTTPSConnection but the server is HTTP (no TLS). So the connection will be refused... Thus we need to fix tests/test_api.py' — and then spent the turn's one action grepping for a phantom instead, because the note said: 'The `serve` function in `orders/app.py` still uses the old `db.HANDLER` reference, which no longer exists after the schema change.' That string exists nowhere in the seed, the workspace, or the final files.
mechanisms.realised_cost: The single most expensive thing in this arm. Three checks lost outright (the HTTP test suite in nemotron/python, the Java build in qwen35 5/5 twice over). Around 25 further calls burned chasing things that were never there — nemotron/python alone ran six greps for `db.HANDLER` across four calls, each returning nothing, and still would not let go.
mechanisms.fix: Take state out of the note. The hand-off note may carry only what was actually done, quoted from real tool results, plus the task. No causes, no file:line, no 'still broken', no 'what remains'. If cria wants a current-state section it must build it by reading the files and running the checks at hand-off time, not by asking a weak model to recall them. Delete the 'this is YOUR OWN prior work' framing as well — it is the thing that makes a guess outrank the disk.

mechanisms.name: cria squeezes the conversation long before it needs to, then tells the model to go re-read everything
mechanisms.what_happens: At every finished step cria folds the whole recent history into a summary and keeps no verbatim tail at all, whatever the size. Runs got squeezed four to seven calls in, on a few thousand tokens, with the window nowhere near full. The file the model just read is gone, replaced by prose plus a line saying not to trust remembered file content and to read from disk instead. The only obedient move is to read it again, so the session re-reads, re-lists and re-derives what it had five minutes ago. cria's own judges suffer the same blindness and re-order commands that already ran and failed.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/java 5/5, call 0239, about 35 minutes into a 45-minute run: 'Let me start by inspecting the workspace to understand the current state of the code. I need to: 1. List the directory structure 2. Read the current Importer.java file...' — three calls after editing that exact file. The note it was reading says: 'before creating any file or redoing a step, INSPECT the workspace (list the directory, read the files that should already exist)'. Six consecutive read/list calls followed and nothing changed on disk.
mechanisms.realised_cost: No check lost directly, but roughly 25 calls of pure re-reading. In two runs it ate the closing minutes: qwen35/java 5/5 spent its last third re-surveying, and nemotron/python 4/4 hit the 60-minute wall with no further edit landing.
mechanisms.fix: In cria/selfcompact.py, `force` at a step boundary lowers the trigger and sets the kept verbatim tail to zero. Remove the boundary-forced squeeze entirely and let the size trigger be the only trigger — the context floor already guarantees the window fits, so this assist is buying nothing and costing the session its memory. If a squeeze does fire, keep the text of files read and commands run this session rather than their names.

mechanisms.name: the hand-off note reports work as finished or tests as passing when nothing was ever run
mechanisms.what_happens: The note lists design choices the model made but never executed as delivered features, and in places states outright that tests pass or that nothing remains. The coder resumes on that and stops testing: it checks that the named code is present rather than that the behaviour is right, and it writes completion summaries that claim more than the file in front of it shows. This is the same generator as the false-broken note, but it fails in the direction that loses points instead of burning calls.
mechanisms.worst_example: gemma4/java 2/2, call 0097. The importer dropped 31,000 of 40,000 rows and the model called it correct: 'the summary shows 9000 rows covering 9000 SKUs were imported, and many duplicates were skipped as expected.' The note it trusted: 'Detecting and skipping duplicate SKUs globally across threads using `putIfAbsent`.' The verifier: 'same totals: False' and '8 runs gave 8 distinct result(s)'.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Five checks lost — three in gemma4/java (faster-but-same-output, the race fix, and the duplicate handling), two in qwen35/ruby where the express-zone point needed the model to write a test and the note told it the session was already complete.
mechanisms.fix: Same root as the false-broken note, same direction of fix: the note carries no verdicts. Specifically it may never say a test passes, a build works, or nothing remains, and it may never list work under 'built' that no command ever executed. Done-ness is cria's gate's job, decided from a real run; the note should not be allowed to have an opinion about it.

mechanisms.name: cria hands out a file list that is filtered, contentless or mis-shaped, and labels it ground truth
mechanisms.what_happens: cria builds a workspace listing and shows different broken versions of it to different readers. Judges get a version filtered down to 'programs', or to files the coder has touched, or to names and byte counts with no content — each one headed 'on-disk ground truth'. The judge has no tools to check, so it states that files do not exist, or ticks off a deliverable that was never created. In one run the listing was accurate but the coder was never shown it at all, so it created a file the task had already provided.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/java 1/1, call 0051: 'We need to test the code now. Let's create a sample feed CSV to test... Create data/feed.csv.' cria's judges were being shown 'data/feed.csv (1211931 B)' at that moment; the coder never was. It overwrote the 1.2 MB benchmark feed with a 520-byte hand-written file, in the wrong column order.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Mostly free — the judge cases changed nothing on disk. One real loss: the destroyed benchmark file left the performance check with nothing large to time.
mechanisms.fix: One listing, read from disk, unfiltered, identical for the coder and every judge, with full relative paths rather than a parenthesised child list. Delete the 'programs only' filter and the touched-files-only view — both invent an absence the label then swears to.

mechanisms.name: denials describe the rule instead of the refusal, so the model believes the wrong thing happened
mechanisms.what_happens: When cria blocks something it writes a general statement of the rule rather than a plain account of that one refusal. A blocked shell line naming only its last part reads as 'the earlier parts ran'. A path rule phrased as 'keep every file you read or write inside the project directory' reads as a rule about the program under test, so the model rewrites working tests to stop using temporary files. And the guard scans heredoc bodies, so a shebang line inside a file's content gets reported as an out-of-bounds write target.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/node 1/1, call 0021. The write went to src/cli.js, inside the project. The denial said: "The path '/usr/bin/env' is outside it; use a path within the project instead." — that path appears only inside the file body as `#!/usr/bin/env node`. The model concluded 'We need to edit the file in place, not write outside' and rewrote a file it had already written successfully.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One check lost: in ternary-bonsai/node a refusal that named a line number but not the parser's actual message led the model to guess, drop an `await`, and ship a test runner that reports ten passes in 39 ms without running anything. Elsewhere about eight calls wasted rewriting tests to dodge a rule that never applied to them.
mechanisms.fix: A denial states three things and nothing else: which single tool call was refused, the raw reason verbatim, and that nothing happened. No rule language, no generalisation, no advice. Scope it explicitly to that call so it cannot be read as a constraint on the code under test, and make the path guard match the command's real targets rather than scanning heredoc content.

mechanisms.name: cria writes the model's next command for it, without checking the command works
mechanisms.what_happens: cria's denials and its steering messages sometimes contain a literal command for the model to run. The model treats a harness instruction as more reliable than its own judgement and runs it verbatim. Neither command was ever validated: one names a binary that does not exist in the environment, the other has its redirections backwards and dumps a build log into the Java source tree.
mechanisms.worst_example: gemma4/ruby 1/3, call 0031: 'Create a `Gemfile` and run `bundle install --path vendor/bundle`.' — copied straight from cria/dirguard.py line 149, which prescribes that exact string. Call 0032 returned exit 127, '/bin/bash: line 1: bundle: command not found'.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Four dead calls in the Ruby run (0032-0035, all exit 127) and a junk compile.log left inside src/ in the Java run. No check lost.
mechanisms.fix: Stop putting commands in cria's mouth. Say what is not permitted and let the coder author its own command — it can see the environment and cria cannot. Remove the prescribed remedies from dirguard's refusal text and the dictated shell line from the steer author.

mechanisms.name: cria deletes search results it judged off-target, destroying an answer the model already had
mechanisms.what_happens: cria decides some search results were not on-topic, removes them, and tells the model what to search for instead — and refuses re-reads of the saved results. The judgement was wrong both times. One model lost the exact dependency coordinates it had just fetched and spent six calls getting them back. The other was steered away from 'add a maintained package' toward 'find a data source', and did the one thing the task forbade: it typed the list into source by hand.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/ruby 1/3, call 0028: 'Based on the search results, I can see the EU member states list... AT, BE, BG...' after cria said: 'Those search results were off-target for this task, so they were removed. Search instead for: EU member states list API or maintained data source for programming.' The task text says don't hand-roll the list. Verifier: 'third-party requires: none'. The list it recited had 26 entries, not 27.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One check lost (the country-zone mapping in qwen35/ruby) and six calls re-fetching a fact that was already on disk in qwen35/java.
mechanisms.fix: Delete this assist. cria should never destroy content the model has already obtained, and it is in no position to rule a search result off-target — it was wrong on both attempts here. If a redirect is wanted at all it can be a suggestion alongside the results, never in place of them.

mechanisms.name: the judge is shown edits with the contents cut out, and assumes the worst
mechanisms.what_happens: When cria renders the coder's history for a supervising judge it elides edit bodies, or truncates the old and new text to about 150 characters each. Two versions of the same file start with the same header, so the judge sees two identical stubs and cannot tell what changed. Asked to rule on a model it is already told is stuck, it defaults to suspicion — it either accuses the coder of faking progress or dictates a change that had already landed one call earlier.
mechanisms.worst_example: gemma4/python, call 0058. The judge wrote 'Wait, I see the current status of `orders/db.py`: def connect(path=DB_PATH)' — the call before had written `def connect(path=None)` and returned 'Wrote orders/db.py'. What the judge saw was '[16] the coder called edit_file — new_string="""SQLite storage for the orders service...' truncated identically for both sides.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Nothing changed on disk in either case; roughly four calls spent confirming work that was already correct.
mechanisms.fix: Give the judge the actual diff of each edit, or the current file contents. Showing the first 150 characters of two nearly identical strings is worse than showing nothing, because it looks like evidence.

mechanisms.name: cria's own control text is fed to a model as if it were somebody's real content
mechanisms.what_happens: Two of cria's internal strings leak into places they were never meant to go. The compaction trigger phrase is routed through the request classifier as though a user had typed it, and the classifier — having no category for it — ruminates until it runs out of tokens and returns nothing. Separately, cria's network-isolated test command is rendered into the coder's transcript as if the coder had issued it, and the coder copies that shell text into its next edit.
mechanisms.worst_example:
nemotron-elastic/python 1/4, call 0046. Meaning to delete a function, the model emitted an edit whose replacement text began '</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
<tool_call>
<function=exec_command>' followed verbatim by cria's own gate command, '__cria_out=$(timeout -k 5 240 python3 -m compileall ...'.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Two calls that produced nothing usable — one empty classifier response, one edit filled with harness plumbing.
mechanisms.fix: cria's internal markers never enter a model's message stream as content. Route the compaction trigger straight to the summarising role and skip the classifier entirely. Render harness-run commands as harness-run in the transcript, distinct from the coder's own tool calls.

mechanisms.name: the model is answered in the shape of cria's shell layer, not the tool it actually called
mechanisms.what_happens: cria lowers tool calls down to shell commands and passes the shell's reply back up. A file-read tool answers with a doubled bash-style error, which the model reads as something strange rather than as a wrong path, so it retries the same path instead of fixing it. In the other direction, an argument that should be a list is lowered as plain text, so a model that carefully corrects its call sends bytes identical to the last one and cannot see why.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/java 2/5, call 0110: 'The read_file command failed with a strange error. Let me try again.' The message was a plain, twice-repeated '/…/mvn_compile.log: No such file or directory' in bash's voice for a tool the model had not called.
mechanisms.realised_cost: About four wasted calls. No check lost.
mechanisms.fix: Parse each argument against the tool's declared type before lowering it, so a list stays a list, and translate failures back into the tool's own voice — one line, the path, and the reason. A model that cannot see the difference between two of its own calls will keep repeating them.

mechanisms.name: cria refused a whole-file read on a small file and prescribed reading it in pieces
mechanisms.what_happens: A 9.6 KB, 253-line Java source file was declared too large to read whole. The model obeyed and read it in three ranges, and so never held the function's signature and its call site on screen at the same time — which was exactly the view needed to spot the mismatch between them. It did not find the bug on that pass.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/java 5/5, call 0243: 'Let me read the full Importer.java file in sections to understand the current state,' after cria said 'Importer.java is large — reading it whole would be truncated (you'd get the head and tail with the middle cut, and act on a false view). Read it deliberately instead'.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Three reads instead of one, and a missed bug on that pass. One occurrence only.
mechanisms.fix: Delete the size-based read refusal. The context floor already guarantees the window fits without truncation, so the premise of the refusal — that a whole read would be cut — is no longer true, and the assist now only blocks the one view that finds cross-line bugs.

mechanisms.name: a test the coder wrote this session was shown to cria's reasoner as if it were the customer's contract
mechanisms.what_happens: cria lists the files the coder has been changing for its supervising reasoner, with no mark saying which of them the coder created minutes ago. The reasoner treated the coder's own freshly written test as a fixed requirement, tried to reconcile it with the task text, and invented a fee the task never mentioned to make the two agree. It then looped on one sentence and returned nothing at all.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/ruby 1/1, call 0027: 'So maybe they omitted the fixed surcharge in spec but intended it. So we can implement a fixed surcharge of 2.5 for express shipments.' The file it was deferring to, test/test_express.rb, had been written by the coder itself at call 0024.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One call that produced no output after roughly thirty repetitions of the same sentence. No check lost — the hidden test decided that point anyway.
mechanisms.fix: The task text is the only contract. cria should not present workspace files to a reasoner as if they carried requirements, and where files are listed at all it should record which ones the coder created this session — that is a fact cria already knows, not a filter.

mechanisms.name: The stuck-detector seat is told the coder IS stuck and must write an order
mechanisms.what_happens: When a detector fires, cria asks a second model to supervise a coder it describes up front as 'flagged as possibly STUCK' and whose thinking it labels 'the reasoning of a model that is currently stuck'. The only alternative to writing an order is the single word ON_TRACK, gated on the coder 'clearly making progress'. Weak models will not certify that, so they hunt for a loop, and when there is none they invent one and give an order anyway. Eleven times the coder was fine: it had just made one or two new, successful, non-repeating moves.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/python call 0043 — the seat ordered: 'Change every function signature to remove the `path=DB_PATH` default'. The project's own seed test calls `db.get_order(oid, path=p)`, and the verifier's injection probe then crashed on the new signature. Prompt text driving it: 'Give exactly ONE concrete next action that differs from the repeated failed behavior. - Command the coder to perform that action NOW with an available tool call.'
mechanisms.realised_cost: One run had working code broken (orders-api python: the path argument the tests pass was ordered removed). The other ten cost redundant orders and re-reads — in gemma4/ruby the coder fixed the bug unaided on its very next turn anyway. The same seat also failed in the other direction once, passing a real 25-call verification loop as on-track.
mechanisms.fix: Make silence the easy answer, not the hard one. The seat may only write a directive if it can quote two identical tool calls from the transcript; otherwise the answer is ON_TRACK. And do not fire the trigger at all while each of the last two turns produced a new tool call with a new result. Honest alternative: delete the flail/stuck steer. In 24 runs it fired on a coder that was not stuck 11 times and its one confirmed save came 26 calls late.

mechanisms.name: The pre-flight research question is answered before anyone has looked at anything
mechanisms.what_happens: Before any code is read, cria asks a model one question: name the external source that must be read first, or say NONE. The same prompt says 'do not use tools, inspect sources' and then prints the workspace file list, so weak models either pick a local file as the 'external source' or take the NONE default. It was wrong in every run where it mattered, in both directions. On a retry cria pastes the rejected answer back into the prompt, so a hallucinated answer gets restated as fact.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/java call 0002 — the answer was 'Read `src/main/java/pipeline/Importer.java` to learn its class structure...', a file listed in the same prompt as already in the workspace. The run then died on an invented CSV API (org.apache.commons.csv.CSVReader, version 1.3.0) that reading the real library docs would have prevented. Prompt text: 'If coding requires reading an external source first, output one sentence naming that source... Do not invent paths, files, URLs, or endpoints not named in the task.'
mechanisms.realised_cost: Two verifier checks lost outright — the maintained EU-membership library in qwen35/ruby and the crate API in ternary-bonsai/rust. One Java run built against a fabricated CSV API. In gemma4/ruby it created a synthetic step that spent seven calls reading two local files.
mechanisms.fix: Delete the pre-flight research step. It is one guess made with no evidence, and the coder discovers the real source when its code fails against the real API. If it is kept: ask only for a library or web page that is not in the workspace, reject any answer whose path appears in the workspace listing, and never feed the rejected answer back on retry — send the rejection reason and the file list only.

mechanisms.name: The judge must name what is broken, but cria withholds the file contents
mechanisms.what_happens: The supervising judge's prompt says plainly that it gets 'changed-file metadata (names, sizes, line counts—NOT contents)', and sometimes it gets '(no check results for this steer)'. It is then required to name an unresolved deliverable or the current error. With nothing to read, it infers from failing test names that a feature is missing and states that guess as an order. In every case the thing it declared missing was already on disk.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/node call 0064 — 'replace the catch block that throws on any non-200 status with a check for status 404 only'. That turned a correct error path into a body-read-twice crash ('Body is unusable') and hid the real bug, a wrong address in the second request. The judge never saw the request URL, only the 404 text.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One run had working error handling destroyed. Three orders in nemotron/python demanded a database column, an index and a route that all already existed. Roughly a dozen calls of the coder re-reading files to disprove the judge.
mechanisms.fix: Never fire this seat without the evidence its question needs: inline the current contents of the changed files rather than their names and sizes, and never send it a prompt whose ground-truth section reads '(no check results)' when a check could be run. A claim that a deliverable is missing should only be allowed after the judge has read that file in the same call.

mechanisms.name: The coder's private thinking is the loudest voice in the judge's prompt
mechanisms.what_happens: cria pastes pages of the coder's own reasoning into judge prompts, last, under a one-sentence warning that it may be wrong. Weak judges weight the most recent and most detailed text, so they adopt the coder's false belief and hand it back as an authoritative order. The judge often has no way to check the belief — no shell, no web — so the only claim about the API in the room is the wrong one it was just given. The supervisor is usually the same small model, so it cannot correct the misconception it is being fed.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/go call 0046 — the judge wrote 'The strange "os.WriteFile returns 1 value" error at line 56 is inconsistent with Go 1.22 (which returns `(int64, error)`), so inspect the actual file bytes... then clear the build cache'. os.WriteFile returns one value; the coder's false claim had been replayed three times inside the judge prompt.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One run effectively lost — ternary/go spent 30 calls chasing file corruption and build caches for a one-line fix and ended stuck. One lost check in nemotron/node, where a passing thought about a `--handle` flag was hardened into a directive and the delivered tool then rejected the positional argument the verifier uses.
mechanisms.fix: Stop putting the coder's raw private thinking into judge prompts. It is the least reliable input and cria places it last, where weak models weight it most. If a trigger needs it, pass one sentence naming what tripped the detector; put the raw tool result or stack trace in its place, and never give it to a judge that must state a fact about a library or a file.

mechanisms.name: The run-it judge is handed a pre-written wrong answer to copy
mechanisms.what_happens: cria asks a model whether the finished work has to be run, and the prompt itself supplies the negative answer and its exact wording: '"nothing runnable has been written yet" is a correct and useful answer, not a failure'. Four times a model finding the question hard copied that sentence back over a Java file with a main() in the list. The same seat also invents commands it has never seen run, because the schema demands a concrete command and a one-line expected output whether or not it knows them.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/java call 0216 — 'The answer is `runs: false` with "nothing runnable has been written yet" in the success field', echoed word for word, while the same prompt listed 'src/main/java/pipeline/Importer.java (9653 B)' under PROGRAMS THAT ACTUALLY EXIST and the same judge had answered runs:true 45 calls earlier.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Three lost checks across the Java runs — the importer was never actually run, which is what the verifier scores. In gemma4/node the judge emitted the literal placeholder `node lookup.js <handle>`, so the live-execution probe reported 'inconclusive'.
mechanisms.fix: Remove the pre-written false answer and its quotable sentence — a weak model copies the cheapest available text. Better upstream: stop asking. cria can find the entry point deterministically (a main(), a bin target, a package.json start script, a build tool's run target) and take the example input from the task text or the README, which is where every correct answer came from anyway.

mechanisms.name: The search supervisor is required to find fault and to name a better query
mechanisms.what_happens: Two judges police searching. One is told drift is 'the #1 way the agent gets poisoned' and must always return a recommendation; the other may only call results on target if they are 'the authoritative documentation, specification, reference, or source'. Both settings force a rejection when the results are simply correct — Maven coordinates are not documentation, and when a query is already fine there is no 'instead' to give. cria then deletes the results file and denies re-reads, so a wrong verdict destroys the answer the coder had.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/java call 0034 — 'The results give dependency info but don't provide the actual API documentation... The task requires authoritative documentation'. The results quoted in its own prompt were '<groupId>com.opencsv</groupId> <artifactId>opencsv</artifactId> <version>5.4</version>' — exactly the dependency the final pom.xml declares.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Two correct result sets deleted and re-reads denied, sending one coder to a 2012 GitHub gist and another back through two more searches. Two calls produced no verdict at all: the judge looped on the forced 'what should it do instead' and the rumination guard aborted the stream. Every occurrence was one model, qwen35, across three languages.
mechanisms.fix: Make the recommendation optional — absent when the query is on target — so the schema stops demanding an 'instead' that does not exist. Change the results bar from 'is this authoritative documentation' to 'do these results answer what the task needs'. Honest alternative: drop the results judge. Deleting search results and then denying re-reads is the only reason a wrong verdict costs anything.

mechanisms.name: The transcript cria shows the judge is not a faithful record
mechanisms.what_happens: Judges reason over cria's rendering of the session, and the rendering loses the deciding detail. Task text is cut mid-sentence, both sides of an edit are truncated at the same offset so a real change renders as a no-op, output redirected to a file shows as an empty result under an exit code, old check output is presented with no mark that the file it ran against has since been rewritten, and a directive shown as an escaped string makes real code look like placeholders. The judge then reasons correctly about a false picture.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/node call 0033 — 'Node.js spawn doesn't reliably fire the close event with a numeric code for processes that call process.exit(). Replace the entire run() helper'. That is false, the helper it condemned is the one in the final workspace, and the only failure evidence in the prompt was stale output from a version of the file that no longer existed.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One correct test helper replaced with a strictly worse one that cannot report an exit code other than 0 or 1. One lost check (the live test never ran). One judge reported a runtime null-pointer crash as a compilation failure, and one gate waved through a directive containing pasteable code.
mechanisms.fix: All of this is cria's own rendering, so it is all upstream. Never truncate the task statement in a judge prompt — it is what every verdict is measured against. Render an edit_file call around the region that differs, not the first N characters of each side. Mark check output stale once the file it ran against has been rewritten. Show the code-dictation gate the raw directive, not an escaped string.

mechanisms.name: The judge's prompt is dressed like a tool-using turn
mechanisms.what_happens: Judges that must answer in plain JSON are sent with the harness tool-call grammar at the top and the coder's tool list pasted in as callable signatures. Weak models mix the two: three times a judge poured its answer fields into the XML template and called a function named `satisfied` that does not exist, producing no verdict at all. Once a judge reached for the coder's edit_file and tried to fix the code itself. Once it read its own read-only restriction as a fact about the coder and claimed the coder had no web tools.
mechanisms.worst_example:
qwen35/rust call 0050 — the response had no content and no tool calls, only '<tool_call>
<function=satisfied>
true
</parameter>' inside the thinking. The same prompt says 'Output fields: - `satisfied` ... - `reason` ... - `proposed_fix`', which reads to the model as a function signature.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Three verdicts lost, each costing two recovery calls, and one of those was then downgraded to a fail-closed 'unverified'. One satisfaction call needed two extra calls to get any answer. The tool-projection case cost nothing.
mechanisms.fix: A judge that must answer in JSON should be sent with no tool-call grammar at all, or the verdict should be a real declared tool it can actually call. Do not let the answer field names collide with what looks like a function name. Describe the coder's abilities in prose, never as callable signatures, and word the judge's own restriction as 'you', not as a bare statement about capabilities.

mechanisms.name: The completion confirmer rules on a claim it was given no evidence for
mechanisms.what_happens: After a done verdict, cria asks a second model whether the claim is consistent. Its prompt carries only the claim and the verdict's own reason — no check output, no transcript. It is supposed to look at the workspace with two read-only tools, but with nothing in front of it a weak model either agrees with the claim or fills the gap from its own memory of the world. It got it wrong in both directions.
mechanisms.worst_example: gemma4/ruby call 0141 — 'INCONSISTENT. The test ... fails because "ZZ" is a valid ISO country code (Eswatini)'. Eswatini is SZ, ZZ is unassigned, and the workspace had just run '17 runs, 17 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors'.
mechanisms.realised_cost: 31 calls after a finished green run, changing nothing. Separately it approved a completion whose delivered file required a dependency the task banned, and approved a claim naming a file its own directory listing had shown missing four times.
mechanisms.fix: Give the confirmer the evidence its question needs: the last check or test output and the workspace listing, in the prompt, with the claim's named artifacts as an explicit checklist. Require any false verdict to name the file it read. If it cannot be grounded, delete it — it is an additive brake, and here it reversed a correct green verdict and rubber-stamped two wrong ones.

mechanisms.name: The self-written briefing states a false current state, and becomes the memory
mechanisms.what_happens: When the session is compacted, cria has the model write a briefing that replaces the history. Three rules in that prompt each caused a failure: identifiers are 'never a fact to keep', concrete errors are 'stable ground truth', and the required slots must be filled with what you have built. So the briefing threw away a third-party class name that was the whole answer, reported errors that a later build had already cleared, and invented accomplishments where the transcript had none.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/java call 0104 — 'The build fails to compile. Concrete errors in Importer.java: - Line 106: incompatible types...'. 'BUILD SUCCESS' was present later in the compactor's own input; the coder then rewrote a file byte-identically to the one that already compiled.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One run rewrote working code from a stale error. gemma4/ruby spent 20 calls rediscovering the class name ISO3166::Country that the briefing had been instructed to discard. In nemotron/java the coder's next turn opened confused by a fabricated file path the briefing had invented.
mechanisms.fix: Three edits to the briefing prompt, all upstream. Exempt names that come from outside the repo — third-party classes, real paths, environment facts — from the rule that identifiers are not worth keeping; the agent cannot rename those. Add recency: an error is current state only if no later run of the same command succeeded. Allow the honest empty answer, 'nothing has been built yet', instead of demanding the slots be filled.

mechanisms.name: cria's own earlier guess comes back to it as evidence and gets confirmed
mechanisms.what_happens: A wrong statement made by one cria model call is carried into a later prompt, often laundered through the coder's reasoning, where it reads as independent evidence. The judge sees its own invention coming back, treats agreement as confirmation, and hardens it. The steer prompt has a rule for this — an earlier note from this system 'is never evidence' — but the rule cannot fire when the claim arrives as the coder's own words or as a stored verdict.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/rust call 0037 — 'all the variant names have been updated to match `toml` v0.8 API: Boolean, Integer, Float, String, Array, Table, None are all used correctly'. Value::None does not exist; the judge had invented that mapping in an earlier steer and was reading it back off the coder. The delivered workspace still fails to build on that line.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One run shipped code that does not compile, with the error blessed by the judge. One run sent the coder on a five-call hunt for an import that was already in the file, because a stored satisfaction verdict said it was missing. The research-step retry, which pastes the rejected answer back in, is a third instance of the same shape.
mechanisms.fix: Tag every line in a judge prompt that originated from a cria model call, and drop those lines rather than labelling them — the labelling rule demonstrably does not hold with weak models. Stop carrying a previous satisfaction verdict into the steer prompt as a finding. Stop echoing a rejected answer back on retry.

mechanisms.name: The stay-inside-the-project rule sent the coder to a cache path that cannot exist there
mechanisms.what_happens: The coder's standing rule is to create, edit and run everything inside the project directory using relative paths. The model applied that to a machine-wide toolchain cache, searched under the workspace for it, found nothing, and concluded the package manager had not cached the crate at all.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/rust call 0029 — 'The registry is empty — it seems the cargo build downloaded toml but didn't cache it in the standard location'. Every search it ran was rooted at <workspace>/.cargo/registry; the crate source was at ~/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-.../toml-0.8.23.
mechanisms.realised_cost: A handful of wasted calls searching an empty path. No check was lost by this turn alone.
mechanisms.fix: Word the rule as a write rule — write only inside the project directory — and say nothing about where it may read. Reads are already bounded by the directory guard, so the prompt does not need to bound them again, and bounding them here made the model reason about a shared cache as if it lived in the workspace.

mechanisms.name: the model decides what the code does by reading it, and nothing ever makes it run it
mechanisms.what_happens: A weak model looks at a line of code, says out loud what it believes that line does at runtime, and is wrong. Nothing in the run forces it to check. Every following step — more file reads, cria's own supervisor, cria's own steer — is another reading of the same text, so the wrong belief is never contradicted and survives to the end of the run. Seven wrong turns, and five of them are the same one misreading: a function written as `def f(x, path=DB_PATH)` looks to the model like it follows the module setting, when in fact the value is frozen the moment the file is imported.
mechanisms.worst_example: slice qwen35/python 4/4, call 0210 — cria's own reasoner, not the coder, gave the order: "The server script needs to override `DB_PATH` before importing the orders module." There is no 'before the import' — importing is what freezes the value. The coder did exactly as told at 0211, and the delivered tests still fail with `assert 111 == 2`.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One run made unwinnable: the orders-api work was delivered still failing, and cria's own supervisor and reasoner repeated the coder's mistake rather than catching it. A second run lost the same check. In ruby it broke working code and burned calls 0036-0050 undoing it. One of the seven (reading `%s` as a safe placeholder) cost nothing — the model reversed itself four calls later.
mechanisms.fix: When a step turns on a claim about what the running program does, the next action cria orders must be a command that prints the answer — ask the running service, print the value — never another file read.
