Today cria's steers answer 'why is this failing?' with 'read the file', which cannot settle a runtime fact. Do not add more supervisor or reasoner calls here: the supervisor is the same model reading the same text and it made the identical mistake at 0108, so extra judgment calls buy nothing.

mechanisms.name: the task lists a normal case in among the broken ones
mechanisms.what_happens: The importer task names five kinds of bad row in one sentence — blank quantities, currency symbols, duplicate SKUs, short rows, embedded commas — and ends by asking for a count of skipped rows and why. Four of those five must be skipped. Duplicate SKUs must be summed: in this feed every SKU legitimately appears five times. A weak model applies one rule to the whole list and throws away most of the data, which also breaks the separate instruction three paragraphs earlier that the speed work must not change what the importer produces.
mechanisms.worst_example: slice gemma4/java 1/2, call 0016 — "Actually, I will skip rows with a SKU that has already been seen in this import. This seems like a safe bet for \"handling\" it." The model had it right six calls earlier at 0010: "I'll assume that if a row has a duplicate SKU we just sum them (as before)". Task text: "blank quantities, prices with currency symbols, duplicate SKUs, rows missing columns entirely ... make sure the summary it prints says how many rows were skipped and why."
mechanisms.realised_cost: Cost the graded speed check in three separate runs — the totals no longer match the seed's, so nothing else in that run can score. In one run 3,210 of 40,000 rows were silently dropped from the money totals.
mechanisms.fix: Fix the task text in this repo (suite/tasks/feed-pipeline-*/prompt.txt): take duplicate SKUs out of the list of broken rows and say plainly that repeat lines for one SKU are legitimate and add up. Do not fix this in cria. A cria-side note about duplicate SKUs would be a hint pinned to one task, which is the exact kind of assist this project has a standing rule against.

mechanisms.name: cria writes the steer from the task sentence instead of from the latest check
mechanisms.what_happens: The steer author reads the task text again, decides what it thinks the task means, and orders a change — without looking at whether the code currently passes, and without seeing the orders it gave earlier in the same run. So it tells the coder to change code that is one test from green, then six calls later reverses itself off the same ambiguous sentence, and after an edit it orders 'read the file' rather than 'run the check', which leaves a dead test failure as the newest evidence in the conversation.
mechanisms.worst_example: slice qwen35/node 1/1, call 0055 — "The task explicitly requires exiting with a non-zero status when a handle can't be resolved, so the tests need to be corrected to match this specification." Six calls earlier the same seat had written the opposite: "The tests failing are all expecting exit code 0 when no handle is provided ... Find and fix the logic". The suite only reaches 22 passing, 0 failing by keeping exit 0.
mechanisms.realised_cost: In node the suite went from 21 of 22 passing to three previously-passing tests broken, and the run spent calls 0044-0059 getting back. In ruby the coder reverted a correct fix on the strength of a stale failure that three read-the-file steers had left standing as the newest test output.
mechanisms.fix: Anchor the steer author to ground truth or keep it quiet. Give it the latest check result and its own earlier orders in the same prompt. If the last edit has not been re-checked, the only order it is allowed to give is 'run the check'. If there is no fresh check result to reason from, author no steer at all — silence beats an order derived from re-reading the task.

mechanisms.name: cria's binary-content guess hides the compiler's error message
mechanisms.what_happens: cria replaces a command's output with the line '[binary content: N bytes — not shown]' whenever the text has enough control characters in it. A build tool printing coloured output is full of escape characters, so a perfectly readable compile error gets withheld. The model then has an exit code telling it the build failed and no error text at all, tries six different ways to see it, and finally abandons the diagnosis and does something unrelated it can at least execute.
mechanisms.worst_example: slice qwen35/java 1/5, call 0028 — "The binary content is being shown. Let me try a different approach to see the actual output." and the emitted action is a web search for "OpenCSV Maven dependency". What it was shown instead of the error: "Process exited with code 0 ... Output:\n[binary content: 3,580 bytes — not shown; binary data cannot be read as text]".
mechanisms.realised_cost: The compile error was never read in that run. The model dropped the diagnosis for roughly twenty calls and at 0045 went on to run a program that had never compiled. The run never got the build working.
mechanisms.fix: Delete the guess. In cria/content_reduce.py, looks_binary() counts every character below 32 as evidence of binary, which makes coloured terminal output look like a blob; cria/writeproxy.py _debinarized() then swaps the model's only diagnostic for a fact line. Withhold output only when the first bytes match a known binary format (binary_kind already does exactly that), and show everything else as text. This is the never-truncate rule applied to the one output that mattered most.

mechanisms.name: old copies of a file stay in the conversation and outrank the real one
mechanisms.what_happens: Every time the model writes a file, the whole file body stays in the replayed conversation as part of that old tool call. Six writes later the conversation holds six full copies of the file and only one of them matches the disk. The model quotes the most-repeated copy, believes the bug it already fixed is still there, and goes back to fix it again. The same replay also feeds the model its own malformed tool-call markers as if they were file text, which sent one run into a circular argument with itself about how many closing tags a file had.
mechanisms.worst_example: slice gemma4/java 1/2, call 0043 — "Currently, the `load` method in my last version is: for (Map<String, String> record : parser) { // This is the problematic line". The disk held the fixed 6,433-byte version written two calls earlier; cria's own file panel says so at 0045 and the build it ran next returned exit 0. The prompt at that point was 101,506 characters carrying six superseded copies of the same file.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Wasted calls in both runs, and one dead turn where the nemotron run produced no tool call and no text at all.
mechanisms.fix: Superseded write payloads must not be replayed. Keep one line per historical write — 'wrote src/main/java/pipeline/Importer.java, 6,433 bytes' — and let only a live read carry file content, so the newest content in the context is always the disk. Same pass strips tool-call framing markers out of any replayed argument text, so the model never reads its own scaffolding as file content.

mechanisms.name: a tool call in the wrong place is thrown away in silence
mechanisms.what_happens: When the model's call does not arrive in exactly the expected shape, cria discards it and gives back nothing the model can act on. In one case the arguments came back with a parse complaint that just quotes the model's own text at it, so the model 'fixes' it and re-sends a byte-identical call. In another the model started composing the call before closing its thinking block, so the whole call was captured as thinking and the turn did nothing.
mechanisms.worst_example: slice qwen35/python 1/4, call 0011 — "Let me fix the JSON format for the plan:" followed by a call byte-identical to 0010. The feedback it had was: "failed to parse function arguments: invalid type: string \"[{\\\"step\\\": ...", which names no fix. Only 0012, which happened to reorder the keys, was accepted.
mechanisms.realised_cost: A duplicate call in the python run. In rust it was worse: the same swallowed-call failure produced empty turns at 0025, 0030, 0045 and 0060, and the run hit the fifteen-minute wall having done nothing. Evidence for the rust case is thinner than for the python one.
mechanisms.fix: One place in cria owns reading what the model emitted. If the response carries no call but the thinking stream contains a well-formed one, take it from there. When arguments genuinely cannot be parsed, the message back must name what to change; echoing the model's own text back to it teaches a weak model nothing and it will re-send.

mechanisms.name: the task line pinned to every turn outranks cria's own steer
mechanisms.what_happens: cria re-pins the task text at the top of every turn. When cria's steer tells the coder to change a test, the coder reads the pinned line 'don't change what the tests assert' as a standing user instruction, decides the steer is asking it to break a rule, and refuses — even though the test in question is one the coder wrote itself, not a seeded one. Nothing in the context tells the two apart.
mechanisms.worst_example: slice nemotron-elastic/ruby 1/1, call 0043 — "Maybe the test expectation is wrong? But we cannot change tests. So we need to adjust our implementation to produce 27.49 for that test case." The steer in the very same prompt said "change the line that asserts Shipping.shipping_cost(\"express\", 4.0, 50.0) to expect 24.99 instead of 27.49", which matches the hidden contract exactly.
mechanisms.realised_cost: The one correct steer of the run was refused, the turn produced no tool call, and the run ended at the fifteen-minute wall with the file reverted. Expensive, but it happened once.
mechanisms.fix: cria knows which files existed when the run started and which the coder created. When a steer orders a change to a test, it must say which of the two this file is, in the steer itself. That is a fact cria already holds, not a new hint. Do not soften the pinned task line to make steers win — a steer that cannot justify itself against the user's own words should not be sent.

mechanisms.name: the workspace path is only ever spelled out in prose
mechanisms.what_happens: The only place the run's working directory appears is inside a sentence of setup prose. The model retypes it from memory, drops the leading slash, and the read fails. It had already made and seen that mistake earlier in the run, but compaction removed the turn that would have taught it.
mechanisms.worst_example: slice qwen35/python 4/4, call 0179 — the emitted read is read_file("tmp/suite-orders-api-py_qwen35_codex_poff_1786522425-9_7l6w90/tests/test_http.py") against a context whose only statement of the path is prose: "Working environment — cwd: /tmp/suite-orders-api-py_qwen35_codex_poff_1786522425-9_7l6w90, shell: bash".
mechanisms.realised_cost: One wasted call. Nothing else.
mechanisms.fix: None. Do not add a path-repair or path-reminder assist for a single wasted call — that is the shape of assist this project keeps having to remove. If the compaction digest is dropping failures the model needs to remember, that is worth watching, but one occurrence is not evidence for it.

mechanisms.group: no cause found in the context — the 216 wrong turns the readers could not trace to anything cria or the task put in front of the model

mechanisms.name: The answer was already in its own prompt and it said the opposite
mechanisms.what_happens: The model states something about a file, a command's output, or an error that the same prompt disproves word for word — or reads a perfectly clear error and picks a cause that error rules out. In the worst cases it decides the compiler, the standard library, or the environment must be broken rather than accept two words of ground truth. This is the kind that most smells of a missed cause: nobody recorded how far up a very long prompt the disproving line sat, or whether cria was still carrying an older copy of the same file below a newer one. Worth one more pass measuring the distance from the claim to its disproof before this is written off as the model.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/go 1/1 call 0038 — decided the Go compiler was wrong: "The Go version is 1.22 which doesn't have `os.WriteFile` returning two values — wait, that's wrong. ... Actually, wait — `os.WriteFile` has always returned `(int, error)`." The compiler line directly above reads "assignment mismatch: 2 variables but os.WriteFile returns 1 value".
mechanisms.realised_cost: Present in all 24 runs and the largest single source of call burn. At least eight verifier checks lost outright: the os.WriteFile belief cost three checks in one go run, an inverted pair of addresses cost the live-API check in the node run, a dropped quantity cost the cart check, and a wrong database diagnosis cost the python integration check.
mechanisms.fix: Mostly nothing — this is the model. The one honest cria lever is what it carries and how fresh it is: when a file changes, replace the copy already in the prompt instead of appending a newer one under the stale one, so the newest text is also the last text. Do NOT answer this by adding a 're-read before you claim' instruction; that text is already in the prompt and the instruction-ignoring kind below shows what happens to it.

mechanisms.name: Makes up a fact about a library or a language and never checks it
mechanisms.what_happens: Version numbers that were never released, class names invented from the library's name, methods that do not exist, wrong rules about how the language behaves, and sums done in its head that come out wrong — all stated with full confidence. Web search and web fetch were in the tool menu on every one of these turns and were used on none of them. This one is genuinely the model: nothing in the context invited any of it, and there was nothing there to be missed.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/java 1/1 call 0013 — "**Add Apache Commons CSV** as a dependency for proper CSV parsing", written into the build file as version 1.3.0. The build says "org.apache.commons:commons-csv:jar:1.3.0 was not found"; 1.10.0 and 1.11.0 were already cached on the machine. That one line failed all five checks.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Five checks in one java run, one in a go run (a shopspring/decimal version that does not exist), the whole rust build (invented toml variants), and steady call burn in every other run.
mechanisms.fix: Nothing — this is the model. Do not re-add a forced research or look-it-up-first step; that was tried and retired. The gate already fails loudly on a dependency that cannot resolve, which is the right and only place this gets caught.

mechanisms.name: Goes in circles
mechanisms.what_happens: Re-runs a command whose output is still on screen, re-reads a file it read three calls ago, re-raises a theory it had already disproved — or the thinking itself collapses into one sentence repeated until the guard cuts the stream. Mostly the model, with a mild smell of a missed cause: cria's repeat notice arrives after the duplicate has run, so on the first repeat nothing had warned it.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/python 3/4 call 0164 — "Maybe the problem is that the schema string includes a backslash before a percent sign? No." restated about fifteen times; the guard aborted the stream after ~8,250 tokens with no output at all.
mechanisms.realised_cost: No check lost anywhere. Roughly fifteen calls of pure burn plus the tokens in the aborted streams — the cheapest kind in this set.
mechanisms.fix: Nothing new. The repeat notice and the rumination guard are already the two things cria can honestly do; blocking a duplicate before it runs would be cria deciding in advance that the model is wrong.

mechanisms.name: Reaches the right answer and then talks itself out of it
mechanisms.what_happens: The model writes the correct diagnosis in plain words and, in the same breath or the next call, argues its way back out and goes somewhere else. This is genuinely the model — the context in these turns contained the evidence for the right answer and nothing at all for the wrong one.
mechanisms.worst_example: gemma4/python 1/1 call 0043 — "If it failed to bind, then the server isn't running, which explains why all requests return 404 (Wait, if the server isn't running, `requests` would throw a connection error, not 404)." The abandoned half was right: a different process held the port, and switching to a free port later fixed it with no change to the routing code.
mechanisms.realised_cost: No check lost by the turn itself, but each one added twenty or more calls, and in two runs the real defect was never revisited before the wall.
mechanisms.fix: Nothing — this is the model, and it is the clearest read on the ceiling in this whole set: it can find the cause, it cannot hold onto it. A steer telling it to go back to what it said would be cria choosing between the model's two opinions with nothing to choose on.

mechanisms.name: Says one thing in its thinking and does another
mechanisms.what_happens: It announces a fix and emits an edit whose before and after text are identical; announces a rewrite and writes the same bytes back; names the file to delete and writes a different one; works out the whole correct fix and then runs a command instead. The reasoning and the emitted call simply disagree. Genuinely the model — this is a gap between deciding and serialising, not anything the context did.
mechanisms.worst_example: nemotron-elastic/java 1/1 call 0065 — the reasoning contains the complete corrected build file ("We need to add <dependencies> after <properties>") and the emitted call is `mvn -q clean compile`. The file was never changed and the run ended broken six calls later.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Three checks (the java build file, a go log field, a python test where only the import line changed) plus a dozen calls.
mechanisms.fix: Nothing to add. cria already answers a no-op edit with "old_string and new_string are identical — this edit changes nothing", which is the honest ground-truth reply; cria cannot know what the model meant to write.

mechanisms.name: Loses track of the edit it just made
mechanisms.what_happens: It believes a fix that landed one call ago is still unmade and re-does it, or undoes it; or believes a line it already removed is still in the file. After an accepted write cria says only "Wrote <path>", so the model never sees the resulting text and its picture of the file drifts. This one smells of a missed cause, and the cause is cria's own thin confirmation.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/ruby 2/3 call 0073 — "my `zone_for` returns \"international\" for unknown country codes, so \"moon\" becomes \"international\"" — the guard that fixed exactly that had landed at 0072 and the tool had answered "Wrote lib/shipping/rates.rb". It reverted its own working fix.
mechanisms.realised_cost: One working file broken and roughly ten calls; no check lost by this kind alone, but it is the feeder for the destructive-edit kind below.
mechanisms.fix: Real cria fix: an accepted write should hand back the resulting text of the changed region instead of the bare line "Wrote <path>" (cria/prompts/write_confirm.txt). That is the tool telling the truth about what it did, not an assist.

mechanisms.name: An edit destroys something that was already right
mechanisms.what_happens: It overwrites a file it never read, reverts a file to its seeded state, drops a parameter without touching the call site, adds a second copy of a test that shadows the first, or narrows a condition a passing test depended on. In several runs the breakage stayed invisible for dozens of calls because nothing checked the edited file.
mechanisms.worst_example: gemma4/go 1/1 call 0006 — wrote a brand-new cart_test.go over the seeded one without ever reading it: "Let's start by creating a reproduction test case." Verifier: "seeded test TestSubtotal from cart_test.go was deleted" — the run's only failed check.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Three checks lost, five runs left holding code that had been working, and in the java run a 44-call gap between the break and the first readable error.
mechanisms.fix: Extend the always-on syntax floor past Python and JavaScript. cria/linterprobe.py checks only those two, which is exactly why a Java arity break survived 44 calls and a Rust one survived to the end. Same kernel-level check, each language's own parser — no task-specific rules.

mechanisms.name: Claims work or a check that never happened
mechanisms.what_happens: The closing summary lists artifacts that were never written, tests that were never run, and verifications that were never performed — often reading its own earlier plan back as a record of finished work. Genuinely the model; nothing in the context asserted any of it.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/node 1/1 call 0043 — "All 10 tests pass. Now let me create the Dockerfile." None of the test bodies ran; the same file in the final workspace exits 0 in 39 ms with the network blocked.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Four checks (the live test, thread safety, a missing regression test, a missing go dependency) and one run that ended on the claim.
mechanisms.fix: Nothing new — the verifier is already the only truth and it caught every one of these. The fix is to stop letting a prose claim shorten a run, which is the two judge kinds below.

mechanisms.name: Does the thing the instructions in front of it forbid
mechanisms.what_happens: Adds a dependency to a task whose whole point is removing one; rewrites a seeded test the user said not to change; builds in a subdirectory when the task says this directory; guesses a URL under a prompt that says do not guess URLs; keeps calling the edit tool after cria says in plain words to stop and write the whole file. Genuinely the model, and it is the strongest argument in this set against writing more rules into the prompt.
mechanisms.worst_example: gemma4/node 1/1 call 0014 — the task in the same prompt says "drop the dependency entirely"; the model: "Okay, I need to install `commander` and then run the tests. I should also update `package.json`." The request_removed check failed on precisely that.
mechanisms.realised_cost: Four checks across three runs, plus the calls spent undoing a project built in the wrong directory.
mechanisms.fix: Nothing — and specifically, do not answer this with more instruction text. The forbidden thing was already stated in the prompt, twice in two of these runs. The safe direction is fewer words in front of the model, not more.

mechanisms.name: cria's own judge passes work its own evidence disproves
mechanisms.what_happens: The satisfaction and confirm judges read the unchanged test file and certify 'with tests' as done, read a hand-typed list and certify 'don't hand-roll the list', or shorten the task into five items of their own invention and drop the two clauses that later fail. Calling these uncaused is misleading: the cause is that cria asks a small model to rule on whether work is finished at all.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/node 1/1 call 0062 — "{\"satisfied\": true, \"reason\": \"... test/run-tests.js includes 10 tests including END-TO-END live API call against 'goose' ...\"}" — it had read the file at 0058, including a runner that never awaits anything.
mechanisms.realised_cost: The most expensive kind per occurrence, because it ends runs. Eight checks lost and five runs stopped early with deliverables still missing.
mechanisms.fix: Delete the assist. A satisfaction/confirm judge running on the same weak model cannot tell finished from claimed — it certified missing tests, hand-rolled lists and a test suite that never ran. The mechanical gate should be the only thing allowed to end a run.

mechanisms.name: cria's own steer invents the specifics
mechanisms.what_happens: The steer author and the judges name files that do not exist, line numbers they made up, symbols they never read, API names they guessed, and workspace paths mistyped from memory — and the coder obeys and chases them. Two wrote a false belief into the carried-forward briefing, where it then sat in every later prompt. Two offered the exact shortcut the task forbade. Again not uncaused: this text is cria's.
mechanisms.worst_example: ternary-bonsai/rust 1/1 call 0031 — "in toml 0.8, the enum variants are different — they use `Boolean`, `Integer`, `String`, and `None`". There is no Value::None; the coder wrote it, and that single invented name is the entire remaining build failure — all four checks.
mechanisms.realised_cost: At least six checks, one run's whole score, plus every call the coder spends reading a file or a line number that does not exist.
mechanisms.fix: Two upstream changes: cria substitutes workspace paths into a directive itself rather than letting a judge type them, and a judge may not name a file, symbol or line it has not read in that same call. If neither can be enforced, delete the free-text steer — it is an assist, and this is the bill.

mechanisms.name: The turn produces nothing cria can use
mechanisms.what_happens: The model writes its tool call, or its entire verdict, inside the thinking channel and leaves the answer empty; calls a tool name that is not in the menu; answers in a JSON shape from some other harness; misspells the one-word verdict; or reaches for the image viewer to read a source file. The round trip costs a full call and buys nothing.
mechanisms.worst_example: qwen35/rust 2/2 calls 0058, 0070 and 0084 — the complete required verdict, "{\"satisfied\": true, \"reason\": \"All requirements verified ...\"}", sits in reasoning_content with content null, three times in one run.
mechanisms.realised_cost: About fifteen dead calls. Each unreadable approval also triggered a recover pass, a reasoning-off retry and a false 'not verified' message to the coder — roughly ten calls each in the rust run.
mechanisms.fix: Two removals. Delete view_image from the coder menu (cria/toolmenu.py): no run used it on an image and four turns wasted it on source code. And do NOT 'fix' the unreadable approvals by reading approvals out of the thinking — cria refuses that deliberately, and fail-open on a missing verdict is the root of every early exit this project has already paid for. The real fix for those four is the one above: stop asking a judge for an approval at all.

critic:
## 1. What is missing — the walk did not explain the pacing result

**Say it outright: the walk never addressed pacing, and the headline as written is partly an artifact of the harness, not a behaviour of cria.**

- The "~23 minutes for every model" is a kill schedule. `/home/jesse/src/cria-shepherd/suite/run.py` sets `wall = milestone_minutes × deliverable_count` and kills a run when the scored snapshot falls below the floor. Deaths land on a grid: 15.8, 16.2, 30.8, 46.2, 60.9 minutes.
- Assisted per-model means: gemma4 23.4, qwen35 25.7, ternary 22.7, nemotron 22.8. They match because they share the grid. Nemotron sat at 15.8–16.2 minutes in 5 of its 6 assisted runs — that is "failed the first floor test five times", not "converged on a pace".
- The real unexplained thing is why assisted runs never stop on their own, and the answer is in the captures, not in any mechanism above: **14 of 24 assisted runs had the coder emit `task_complete`, and cria kept them running 3 to 69 more calls. 409 of the 2,178 calls the readers read — 19% of the corpus — happened after the coder had already declared done.** Worst: nemotron/node declared done at call 7 and ran to call 76 and the 15-minute kill; qwen35/rust declared at 29 and ran to 98. The baseline arm has no `task_complete` at all — those runs end when the model stops.
- **The score-over-time data already exists and the walk did not use it.** Every row in `/home/jesse/src/cria-shepherd/suite/results/results.jsonl` carries a `milestones` array — the verifier's score on a copy of the workspace every 15 minutes. At that resolution the verdict is split, not "clock catches it mid-edit":
  - flat plateaus: gemma4/java 2 at 15m and 2 at 42m (baseline 4); qwen35/python 3 at 15m and still 3 at 60.9m after ~170 more calls.
  - reached-then-lost: qwen35/java 2 at 30m (exactly its baseline final) then 0 at 45m; ternary/python 1 at 15m then 0.
  - real late gains: gemma4/ruby was at 3 at minute 45 and finished 5 at minute 59. The campaign's single biggest win was earned in the last quarter of the clock, which is direct counter-evidence to "cut it off sooner".
- Caution the walk also missed: ternary/python **baseline** went 3 at 15m to 1 final. Score destruction is not cria-only.

## 2. Java is under-explained

- The -80 rests on two runs. ternary and nemotron score 0 in both arms on Java — floor effects contributing 0.
- **The mechanism the walk calls the largest single cost in Java fires just as often without cria.** Prompts carrying `[binary content …]`, BASE vs CRIA: gemma4 13/30 vs 86/112; qwen35 47/69 vs 212/275; ternary 21/36 vs 13/37; nemotron 0/9 vs 45/71. gemma4 scored 4/5 in the baseline arm with 13 blanked Maven outputs. The ANSI/binary bug is real and worth fixing, but it is a constant across arms and cannot explain a delta.
- gemma4/java has a genuine cria-authored cause on the table (the duplicate-SKU steer that shipped into the deliverable). qwen35/java does not — the walk itself attributes the fatal `accumulate` arity break to the model. But the milestone trail shows that run at 2.0 at 30 minutes, equal to its baseline final, and 0 at 45. **cria reached the baseline result and then went past it and broke it.** That is the cleanest instance of explanation (a) in the whole corpus and no mechanism names it.
- So the open Java question is not "which steer" but exposure: 275 calls versus 69 in the same file, with the compiler invisible in both arms. Nobody tested that.

## 3. The 216 untraced turns

- The ratio is not believable as published, on the walk's own words. Two clusters filed under "no cause found" say in their own text that the cause is cria's: "cria's own judge passes work its own evidence disproves" (16) and "cria's own steer invents the specifics" (19). Re-filing those alone makes it 436/181.
- The deeper problem: **the readers read 2,178 calls and every one of them was assisted.** Zero of the 24 baseline runs were read. "The model does this anyway" was asserted, never measured. Without a per-call base rate, "no cause found" and "the model" are the same sentence.
- Kinds most likely to have a cause nobody found, in order:
  1. **"The answer was already in its own prompt and it said the opposite" (55).** The readers flagged this themselves. Nobody recorded how far up the prompt the disproof sat, or whether a superseded copy of the same file sat below the current one — which is exactly the traced mechanism in the gemma4/java entry (six copies of one file in a 101K-character prompt).
  2. **"The turn produces nothing cria can use" (15).** The tool-call grammar, the sampling settings and the JSON field names are all cria's. `/home/jesse/src/cria-shepherd/suite/replay.py` already measures `tool_ok` and `verdict_ok` on captured calls.
  3. **"Loses track of the edit it just made" (7).** Its own entry names the cause — the bare `Wrote <path>` confirmation. It should not be in this bucket.
  4. **"Goes in circles" (15).** The repeat notice arrives after the duplicate; the first repeat is unwarned.
  5. "Makes up a library fact" (31) is the one most likely to survive as genuinely the model — but only a baseline rate can say so.

## 4. What would settle it — five things, in order

1. **Per-call score curve for the ~10 pairs with a nonzero delta and more than 15 minutes of assisted wall.** Replay each `write_file`/`edit_file` from `~/.cria/calls/<session>/*coder*.response.json` onto a copy of `/home/jesse/src/cria-shepherd/suite/tasks/<task>/seed`, running that task's `verify.py` after every write. Output per run: peak score, the call number and minute of peak, final score. (a) predicts peak ≥ the baseline twin's final, reached well before the wall. (b) predicts peak = final, below baseline.
2. **One column derived from that: the assisted workspace's score at the baseline twin's wall-clock time.** If it is at or above the baseline score, the clock is the whole story. If it is below, the extra work is worse work. That single column answers the campaign's headline.
3. **Termination audit.** For each assisted run, the call index of the first `task_complete`, what cria did with it, and whether the score moved afterwards. The first half is already measured (14 runs, 409 calls after declaration); the missing half is whether any of those 409 calls ever earned a point.
4. **Read a control.** Six baseline runs, one per language, from the models that score above zero — counting only the three untraced kinds above, per call. This is the cheapest way to find out whether 216 is a real number.
5. **Per-arm rate check on every mechanism claimed as expensive.** The grep I ran for the binary marker, repeated for the stale-checks banner, the compaction briefing and the elided-content marker. Any mechanism that fires at the same rate in both arms is a cost to fix, not an explanation of the delta — and at least one headline mechanism has already failed that test.
